provenance.authorAccess: Scenario author did not read source implementation, v1 cases, predictions, annotations, or evaluation reports.
provenance.method: 240 separately written pair narratives across 12 procurement families; a deterministic serializer supplies record IDs, synthetic document hashes and asynchronous entry timestamps.
provenance.documents: Receipt hashes represent fictional uploaded files, not reconstructed source documents. Shared files may contain multiple payable lines. Different hashes may represent copies, rescans, corrected forms, or different documents.
provenance.scope: Scenario narratives can include operational facts unavailable in predictor records. No supplier identity or receipt line allocation is added to the persisted record schema.
provenance.annotationStatus: Unannotated. No author decision key, evidence-tier key, prediction, or model score is included.
limitations: Fictional narratives and common author conventions are not operational prevalence evidence.
Transaction histories can remain unresolved; narratives intentionally do not guarantee binary certainty.
Creation timestamps are synthetic entry times and must not be read as service dates.

splitPolicy.groupIsolation: Each procurement dossier has a unique groupId; no family or group appears in both splits.
splitPolicy.annotationProtocol: Separate blind reviewers receive shuffled id/scenario/left/right packets only; category, split and supplyFamily are withheld.

cases.scenario: The office wing curtains were cleaned in April and again after smoke damage in August. Both services were entered together when the office reopened.
One claimant remembers buying a measuring wheel. Another remembers paying a repair bill. The vouchers have no itemisation, and neither recollection has been verified.
The same fifty-bag purchase was first described as replacement material and later by the bag label. The store’s signed receipt number matches on both records.

The buyer submitted the original receipt and the stores clerk submitted its photocopy. A crease hides part of the number on the copy, transcribed as MT-89 instead of MT-39; both show the one collection.
The supervisor submitted the till slip and the storekeeper submitted its emailed image for the same six-pair collection.

left.description: Six pairs steel-toe boots, mixed sizes, stores.

right.description: Safety boots for six unloading staff.

cases.scenario: Husk disposal and bran bagging were separately ordered services. A carbon sheet includes both, but each record represents a different line and different amount.
The catering lead and store clerk both entered one three-pot purchase. Each used the same invoice number and scan; the receiving ledger records three pots total.

right.description: Three large stainless cooking pots, 30 L.

cases.scenario: Two farmer groups each brought 500 kg on the same day. They paid separately; the app wording omits the group names.
A reimbursement envelope and a laundry account statement might describe the same service. The envelope is undated, and the statement covers three visits without itemising them.

left.description: Uniform wash and repair, depot staff.

cases.scenario: Both uploads are cropped photographs of a faded receipt. The visible marks could read E-418 or E-478. No one has established whether the crops show the same paper.

left.description: White epoxy marking compound, depot collection.

right.description: White epoxy marking compound, depot collection.

cases.scenario: A volunteer’s note lists a can opener and peeler. Another note lists a can opener, peeler and whisk; neither states whether it is a combined summary or a separate purchase.
The coordinator paid at collection and the treasurer later entered the same charge from a card statement. The statement reference and laundry job number are different identifier systems.
The reusable bags were purchased separately from the processing labour. The office attached the same mill invoice, which itemises both charges.
A supplier account number was entered as the transaction reference. Both receipts contain that number, but they are for separate dated mat exchanges.
Two handwritten vouchers may concern the same volunteer’s travel or different volunteers’ fees. Neither voucher names a person, session or date, and no organiser remembers the payment.
The site book names two bridge decks but these entries contain neither deck name nor a receipt. The purchasing officer cannot say whether the second entry was a copy or a second collection.

left.description: Black primer for bridge deck line work.

right.description: Black primer for bridge deck line work.

cases.scenario: The cobbler processed three pairs in June and another three in July. The app was updated late, so both records were created in August; service dates are retained.
The organiser and treasurer describe the one hired cabinet differently. The rental invoice names the same cabinet serial and hire docket in both uploaded copies.
Each desk had its own interpreter for the same afternoon. The agency used one programme reference, but the desk locations remain in the app.
The session lead and finance officer entered the same interpreter invoice. The attendance sheet records one interpreter working the one session under booking INT-401.
The buyer negotiated a discount on one batch after finding uneven growth. The original receipt and reduced replacement receipt were both entered; no second batch was delivered.
The same seven sacks were weighed in and the receipt was later scanned again after being stamped collected. The stamped copy preserves the same job number and charge.
The compass set was bought for the geology team. The feet were bought three weeks later for the mapping team. A reused upload mistakenly attached the compass receipt to both entries.
The standby reservation was converted to a confirmed booking at no further charge. Both forms show the same payable total, and the reservation fee was credited in full.
The laundry collected separate loads from the two halls and charged each load equally. Its driver combined both service lines on one day sheet.
A clerk scanned the receipt before it was stamped paid. The later scan shows the paid stamp; both refer to the pack collected at 14:20 on docket NB-51.

right.description: Waterproof field notebook pack for chainage crew.

cases.scenario: The two capacities were purchased for separate workstations. They cost different amounts and appear as separate lines on one consolidated receipt.
The delivery was booked in kilograms by the store and in sealed bags by finance. The depot’s log ties both entries to weighbridge ticket AG-62.
The orchard clearing needed three truck trips. These entries are for the first and second trips, each independently weighed and billed.
A volunteer entered the purchase from a phone receipt. The project accountant later entered the bank transfer receipt, whose reference is the payment ID rather than the nursery order.
The advance was handed to the crew lead before purchasing. The later entry records the material charge from the trip; the advance has not been reconciled against several receipts.

right.description: Line paint and bead collection for eastern bypass.

cases.scenario: The pot-lid and complete-pot purchases were made separately. The buyer mistakenly attached the pot-lid receipt to the complete-pot entry, while their payment references differ.
The reserve plants and installation plants were separate orders for different purposes, each paid on a different invoice. Identical unit pricing produced equal totals.
The trainers and guards are separate nursery accessories bought on different days. A reused photograph accidentally attached the trainers receipt to the guards entry.
The receipt was photographed flat and later folded, producing different file digests. Both photographs show the same service ticket and payment stamp for the only blanket collection that month.
One voucher may cover a volunteer’s portion of a pooled order. The other may be the entire pooled purchase, but the coordinator has no contribution ledger or itemised receipt.
